body_en_plain:
August, 1994      Page Reply


 How to write to us...02     -
 Bill Clark...........03    07
 Chris Ingram.........13    20
 Phil Muscart.........24    25
 Chris Norfolk........27    30
 N.J. Shelley.........33    34
 Malcolm Perry........36     -
 Malcolm Goodman......43    48
 Leif Mortensen.......52    55

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

Bill Clark, BARROW-IN-FURNESS


Dear Ron & Brian,
(or is it Brian and Ron?)

Please can you answer the foll-
owing questions for me as I am
experiencing some difficulties..

1. On the +3 B: drive, is there
any way of CATaloguing more than
64 files?

2. A while back I wrote to you
asking if there were any more
hidden messages on the +3. I
haven't had an answer yet.

3. How do I convert TASWORD to
run solely on Drive B:?


4. In past issues of OUTLET, you
refer to something called
M3UNLOCK for unlocking a Multi-
face. Is it still available, how
much and where from?

5. How can I get an original
copy of OUTDEX as I don't have
one and your OUTLET programs
have it listed but it prompts me
to put in an OUTDEX disk?

6. How about telling me a bit
about yourselves. How many mem-
bers do you have. Which is the
most: Speccy/SAM/PC, etc.?

7. Is there a program available
on disk for the +3 to list
telephone codes in numerical
order and also is there a
similar program for postcodes?

8. I'm also after a program that
will enable me to read bar codes
and a FAX receive program though
I would need it explained as to
how it worked.

9. After numerous problems I
have blown a couple of computers
and power supplies. On the
computer all I get is a blank
screen with a border. Do you
know what it may be that is
wrong? Also I keep blowing power
supplies and having to replace
fuses and transistors. Why is it
the transistor always blows
before a fuse? Surely it would
be more convenient to blow a
fuse? Can you explain how they
work and produce a diagram or
something for the +3 power
supply?

Anyway, my problem is now solved
to some extent as I've bought a
secondhand +3 and I am running a
B: drive from a separate power
supply.

         Best regards,

           Bill Clark

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

1. The standard +3 format only
allows for 64 files in the CAT
so a special format is needed. I
have some code and information
recently received on this but it
looks immensely time-consuming
to get into working order and
has, regrettably, to join a huge
queue of jobs to be done! This,
presumably, is also aimed at the
standard 3" drive. If you have a
3.5" DD drive then it probably
will not work as it is anyway.


2. I replied to your request for
hidden messages last month on
Page 46 of OUTLETTERS. Sorry,but
I just don't know of any more!


3. You do not say which Tasword
version. If it is Tasword 2 then
at the end of line 15 but just
BEFORE the GO TO 5, insert...

     LOAD "B:" : SAVE "B:":

          ...then resave Tasword
with the 't' option in the menu
within Tasword.

Alternatively, enter the above
as direct commands (or in a pre-
loader program) and then load
Tasword FROM drive B.

Tasword 3 appears to force use
of Drive A even if loaded from
B so the only way is to load it
from Drive A and then press the
symbol + B option at the main
menu.

4. M3UNLOCK was produced by...

            TNYSOFT
        27 BAYSDALE ROAD
             ASHBY
           SCUNTHORPE
        SOUTH HUMBERSIDE
           DN16 2QE

        ...for `9.95 or `6.95 if
you sent your own disk. I do not
know if TNYSOFT still supply it
or if they are still at that
address (our review was in Issue
40 which was December,1990!) but
you might try sending them an
SAE and ask them to confirm they
still can provide it before you
part with any money.Our reviewer
recommended them for their serv-
ice and the product.


5. If you read the whole message
when trying to load OUTDEX you
will see it says that MASTERFILE
is in Issue 75.You load the data
and resave it the whole program
as OUTDEX and then each month it
can be loaded direct from the
CONTENTS page.You then merge the
monthly data from that issue and
resave the whole program again
as OUTDEX.

6. We had around 3,000 'members'
on our database I think,the last
time I looked but of course,they
don't all take OUTLET monthly.We
supply less than 500 a month now
and these are mostly +D and PC
which is growing.The +3 are down
to only about 50 or 60 I think
and there are only a handful of
tape readers.

7. We had telephone codes in our
Issue 45 in ADDENDERS. They are
in MASTERFILE format(so you need
MASTERFILE from Issue 75). They
are files STD2 to STD9. I do not
know of any similar list of post
codes. I believe most post codes
cover just a few addresses so
the full list must have millions
of entries!

8. We did have a bar code reader
program or listing for the SAM
but I can't find it now. I have
a feeling it needed more work on
it and it joined the queue of
work waiting to be done and
probably got abandoned when the
SAM version ended. If I find it
I will see if it can be made to
work on a Spectrum.


9. Well, you know more about the
hardware side of computers than
I do so I can't help you direct
but hopefully some of our more
technically-minded readers may
be able to make suggestions. My
best guess is that your B drive
should have had a separate PSU
from the beginning and that is
what kept blowing fuses.

                   Brian

From Chris Ingram, MALAWI

Dear Brian

Thank you for including my lett-
er in Outlet 82 and the comments
thereon. Thank you also for
Outlet 83 which I collected this
week. I'm sorry not have written
earlier but a bout of 'flu,added
to the usual workload, made life
difficult for a while.

Of the suggestions you gave me
to choose the default report on
a MASTERFILE file the one where
two extra lines are added to the
Basic works well. I even, after
a few false tries and some blue
language, managed to make it do
the same when the file is saved
as part of the program.

I usually keep two copies of
each file saved as a program for
ease of loading and for User
Basic, and another two discs of
back up files only.


When I reached Page 26 in your
reply I found myself reading
part of my own letter again. Did
you notice this? I assume it was
extra and didn't overwrite
something you told me: Page 27
seemed to follow on all right.


The alteration to Wordmaster to
access the correct drive without
cataloguing first only worked if
I added CAT d"""", CAT*"""" left
it on the same drive.


You say you never thought much
of VERIFY but it does sometimes
show up a sector error which was
not picked up when saving.

Thank you, also,to Malcolm Perry
for his contribution in Outlet
83. I'll remember his tip about
the cotton buds and methylated
spirit. At the moment I've had
(touch wood)a reasonably trouble
free few months. Maybe in the
cooler weather the heat is
dispersed more readily, but I'll
try the hair dryer trick if that
sort of crash happens again. I
have a short length of ribbon
between the computer and +D
which I originally bought to
attach my DKTronics keyboard to
the Disciple. I find that more


reliable than the direct conn-
ection - less vibration from the
keyboard, I suppose. Certainly
the ones at school used by small
children crash quite frequently.


Thanks for explaining the diff-
erence between the +D and Disc-
iple LPRINT command and why POKE
@11 won't help. Not being tech-
nically inclined I'll just have
to live with it.

The same applies to Miles
Kinloch's detailed hardware fix
for the sticky keys. Something
else I can live with and various
bits of code I have, do the job
when I can remember to load
them.


I think our electricity supply
is 220 volts, but don't have the
means to check. It would explain
why the 350ma PSUs did not work
well but the 500ma one does. We
do get problems with electricity
supply here; I believe most of
the domestic supply equipment is
old and is certainly unreliable:
during the rainy season power
cuts are almost a daily feature
of life. At least being hydro-
power we aren't contributing to
the greenhouse effect!

I've tried DISCTIDY's Gap Closer
(Outlet 83) without success.This
was left out of Catloader 2 so I
thought it would be useful. If I
relate what happened it may help
you or the author to pinpoint
the problem...

A disc had 8 programs left on it
after a Catloader Erase session:
1 2 3 4 5 26 44 46. On running
Gap Closer (both directly from
Outlet and Extracted program
behaved the same), the screen
after the initial flurry of
counting showed me:

  oldfile 75
  oldslot 87

It then moved 26 to 6, 44 to 7,
and 46 to 8. So far, so good.
However it then continued moving
imaginary files: 81 to 9,
82 to 10, 88 to 11, 89 to 12,
90 to 13, 91 to 14, 92 to 15,
93 to 16, 98 to 17 and
99 to 18 whereupon it crashed:
580:3 Integer Out of Range.


I hope one of your boffins can
sort this out: I was using a +2
with Betados.

 Best wishes to all at Outlet,

          Chris Ingram

PS Andy Moir kindly sent me the
Betterbytes Disc Manager for +D,
which unfortunately doesn't work
with my BetaDos system. Nor have
any of the "fixes" so far
published in FORMAT helped. The
Configurer doesn't recognise the
system unless it's the same
length as +GDOS.

Brian Cavers to Chris Ingram

That reprint of part of your own
letter on Page 26 of my reply is
probably due to a glitch in our
text compressor coupled with my
not having time to check all the
text THOROUGHLY once in OUTLET.

I used to edit text, check it
again in the wordprocessor then
compress it into OUTLET and then
check EVERY single word a third
time and finally, if the whole
thing had to be re-edited for
one or two errors I checked it
all again a FOURTH time! Now I
cannot find the time to do it
that thoroughly and only double
check it in the wordprocessor
with a third (quick) check in
OUTLET.

The result is that scanning the
text rapidly for obvious errors
I might not take in the overall
meaning - the pages were correct
for grammar and form etc - even
the pages are numbered automat-
ically 'as they are'.

Unfortunately, I don't keep the
original text of my replies for
more than one month but I don't
think anything was lost. When I
have previously trapped such an
error at the compression stage
it is usually a re-insertion of
a previous page - not an over-
write. It's caused by the text
file being too big for our text
compressor - which I do normally
split first but maybe overlooked
here.


Sorry, yes - obviously I should
have said CAT d"""" and not the
CAT *"""" which just forces the
current drive to er... become
the current drive! Not much use
really!

Regarding VERIFY, what I meant
was that in the time spent using
VERIFY one may as well just save
the file again on another disk.
I would prefer two unverified
copies of a file on separate
disks to a single verified copy
on one disk any day of the week.
I think that more errors occur
at a later stage when even a
verified file can be lost due to
an overwrite - or even a bent
disk or the proverbial spilt cup
of coffee.


Hopefully,DISKTIDY's author: Mr.
Baumann can suggest a solution
to the GAP CLOSER error but it
may be a DOS glitch. That LOAD@
and SAVE@ is wicked.We have some
POKEs coming up in a future OUT-
LET about this which may help.

                      Brian

From Phil Muscart, LIVERPOOL

Dear Ron,

Could you tell me what specific-
ations would be needed to run
the PC OUTLET as I will be up-
grading to 3.5" format disk soon
and want to continue my support
for OUTLET. Also, is it possible
to run OUTLET's Spectrum version
under emulation on the PC?

Many thanks for all your help.

         Phil Muscart

Brian Cavers to Phil Muscart

The PC OUTLET needs a 3.5" high
density drive, a VGA display and
1 meg of memory. That is the
minimum standard for ALL new PCs
- they virtually all come with
VGA,a 3.5" HD drive and at least
one meg of memory.Unless you are
buying second hand you should
have no problem. I do not know
too much about laptops though.It
may be that certain types will
not run OUTLET but your average,
normal, modern PC should not be
any trouble. About one third of
the standard 1 meg is used for
screen memory, system routines
etc, leaving 640K - and say,100K
of that may be in use running
"support" programs leaving 500K
for OUTLET which is fine.

The new version of the Lunter PC
Spectrum emulator which should
be available in the next few
months can directly run the +D
version of OUTLET, straight from
a +D or Disciple disk in the PC
3.5" drive - whether DD or HD.It
cannot guarantee, of course,that
every program will run perfectly
but it comes close! You can even
print as normal and save files
back to disk just as if you had
a +D!

As soon as we hear it is defini-
tley available we shall announce
it in OUTLET.

                       Brian

Brian Cavers to Chris Norfolk

Thanks, Chris.

If you can load programs from a
disk on the +3 then it sounds
like there is nothing wrong with
the drive so you should be able
to save. It is likely you are
just doing something wrong. Let
me know exactly what you are
doing to save and any error
message on the screen.

Points to note: You can only
save to +3 disk in 128K mode. It
is essential to have a disk with
blank space on it and it must
NOT be write-protected (this is
either a sliding or push button
at the inside edge of the disk).


New disks MUST be formatted be-
fore you can save on them. You
do this by putting your disk in
the drive and typing...

          FORMAT "A:"

    ...BUT YOU MUST DOUBLE CHECK
AND MAKE SURE IT IS A NEW DISK
OR ONE THAT IS NOT IMPORTANT AS
ANYTHING ON THE DISK WILL ALL BE
ERASED!


In any disk OUTLET you have,load
the CLIP art program,put a blank
disk in the drive and press S to
SAVE. Enter a filename and then
the program asks for the drive.
Enter A and it should save. Let
me know the result.


How do you access press and news
agencies with your +3? It sounds
interesting. Do you log on with
a modem or what?

                         Brian

From Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Ron and Brian.

I have a few notes arising from
various letters in Issue 83...

UNIDOS "KEYWORD" rejection: I
discovered this "problem" when I
first started using the DOS and
thought that my own solution of
modifying the OUTLET basic so it
would load the CODE suffix files
[used in early issues - Ed]
WITHOUT having to rename every
file may be of interest. If you
did rename the files on the disk
then there is also the problem
that all the file names in the
look-up table in the menu rout-
ine also have to renamed.


The files with the CODE suffix
are in the main text files that
are loaded from the BASIC rout-
ine that forms the menu screen.


A relative small mod overcomes
most of the problems although
there may be odd programs that
after loading the BASIC go on
and load a CODE file and so will
need to be altered on similar
lines.


Typical loading routines look
like...


LOAD d*; C$(PEEK NIF) CODE  or..
LOAD d*;(CODE K$ - CODE "@")CODE


Using Issue No.15 as an example,
the BASIC to load the code file
is in line 300 and needs to be
changed to:


  LOAD d*;C$(CODE K$-CODE "@",
  TO 9) +"*" CODE.


The idea is possible because the
"CODE" keyword character part of
the name is always at the 10th
position. The modified loading
routine therefore removes the
original CODE character from the
file name and substitutes "*"
(wild card - you could use "?"
instead) so when loading a file
the 10th character in the file
name on disk is ignored.


Obviously the files still load
OK on GDOS. Because each issue
uses a fairly standard block of
code, all that is needed is to
write a new line and save it to
disk. It can then be MERGED into
each issue to replace the exist-
ing line and the modified BASIC
resaved (look around line 9980
for the +D erase and resave).


Warning...

Before doing the MERGE, check
that the line is the same
because I have found some varia-
tions in the BASIC layout as
issues progress. However, the
principle of the mod is the
same.


While on subject of ROMS, I, for
a number of reasons of incompa-
tability, have not made full use
of UNIDOS and tended to leave
the GDOS ROM in place. The
"advantages" I can live without,
the "disadvantages" were a
problem. At least "upgrades"
that only modify the BOOT file
are no real problem as it is
easy to BOOT with either system.

I am at moment considering three
options to overcome the problems
and enable me to have both ROMs
installed and simply switch in
one required.I have decided hard
switching is all I need as it is
most unlikely I would need or
want to switch ROMs from soft-
ware and that each needs a diff-
erent BOOT file.

Option 1 is to make up a PCB
with sockets to take both ROM
chips that plugs into existing
ROM socket (takes up lot of
room, covers will no longer fit
properly but things can be
restored to original).

Option 2 is to solder the two
ROMs together leaving appropr-
iate pins free to select which
required (two dud ROMs if things
go wrong! Cover will still not
go back on, not easily restored
to normal).

Option 3 put both ROM codes onto
one IC that plugs into existing
socket with few mods. approp-
riate half selected by simple
switching.


Option 3 is my favoured option.
I have yet to consult a local
friendly firm to see if they can
do this and, more importantly,
at what cost. The method allows
easy restoration to normal and
the original ROMS are left
intact and safely stored).



QL RGB socket...

YES, this is the same as the
Spectrum for RGB, (pins 7,6,8)
comp sync (4) and earth pin (2).
The output is at 5V TTL level so
similar to the 128 and +2. The
+3 is at SCART (1V) level.

               Malcolm Perry


From Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS

Dear Brian/Ron,

Due to a severe shortage in the
ideas department I thought I'd
examine those CODE-IN-REMs that
are a regular feature of OUTLET
programs.

My findings are that you use the
sysvar 'NEXTLIN' and a negative
offset to find the code start
address. This address is always
(?) the first location after the
CHR$ 128 that you use to 'hide'
the code. I also note that some-
times you use leading zeros so
as to be able to adjust the
offset anywhere between 0 and
9999 without upsetting things.


However, have you considered
sysvar CH-ADD at 23645/6 as a
reference? eg..
9993 RANDOMIZE USR VAL"PEEK
23637 +256 * PEEK 23638 - 0099":
REM CODE
This moves the assembler file
(below) to 60000. After a USR
command, an entry to the code
sys var CH-ADD points to where
the colon is that precedes the
REM (or RETURN command). If you
allow NN bytes in the REM for an
identifier name and the flashing
code as well as CHR$ 13 + 128
then...
LD HL,(23645); find colon
LD BC,NN     ;get forward offset
ADD HL,BC    ;get 1st code byte
JP (HL)      ;go to it.
..will kick your code into life.


You would then have no more neg-
ative offsets to calculate!!

All you need is to get those 8
bytes of code into RAM using
NXTLIN(!)and then any subsequent
code-in-rem in that program can
be started by calling the
address in RAM where those eight
bytes of code are stored. Thus
you'd have line 9993 as previous
which moves the 8 code start
bytes to say 60000 then...

9994 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 1
9995 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 2
9996 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 3

  ...and thus you have a generic
method of finding that first
code byete following CHR$ 128.


I hope yu can follow all this.If
not,let me know and I'll try and
clarify or even put a working
demo together.


I note Chris Oliver made mention
of my STRIPPER program in OUT-
WORK #83 as being in the current
issue. I suspect he is thinking
ahead (?) as I can't find it.


Can I just mention your AUTOLOAD
program? If you examine line 9
you'll note a GO SUB 1001: GO
SUB 1002. Why not remove the
RETURN in 1001 and let the GO
SUB 1001 process lines 1001 and
1002.



In like vein, that GO SUB 1E3
plus GOSUB 1005 could be cleaned
up by renumbering line 1000 to
1004,removing the RETURN in 1004
and then a single GO SUB 1004
will handle lines 1004 and 1005.
It saves a few bytes which helps
on +3 disks.

I think I've said enough.

                Malcolm

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman


Those are interesting ideas but
I don't think they merit the
change...

The advantages I think you see
in your code-in-rem method are..

1. Code lines use less memory.
2. No need to calculate offset.

However, No.1 is only effective
if one has several lines because
of the extra setup line and No.2
is ineffective because we don't
actually need to calculate the
offset! It is done automatically
and effortlessly by REMSTORE in
Issue 6!


The disadvantages of your method
are...


1. More complicated: You still
   have all the original lines
   PLUS an extra line PLUS extra
   code in memory.

2. Extra check needed to see any
   new code doesn't clash with
   setup code and subsequent
   hassle renumbering ALL the
   lines if set up code has to
   be moved.

3. Not self-contained. With our
   present method, all REMs are
   totally self-contained and
   need not rely on links with
   another line/code.


Your method might be preferred
if one had dozens of code lines
and used a variable for the
address of the setup code, eg..

     RND USR X:RETURN:CODE

     ...which not only saves a
bit more memory but if the code
needed moving slightly one need
only alter the value of X.

As it is, our current method is
reasonably trouble-free and you
know what they say, if it works,
leave it alone! Well, something
like that anyway! You know what
I mean, unless there is a BIG
advantage in a change or the
present method causes some great
hassle then I say let thing lie!


Your idea of merging of GOSUBs
in the loader program is OK in
theory but the GOSUBs are self-
contained so can be removed or
added to with ease at present.
However, if you take out a
RETURN here and there, one may
get an error with any future
changes if it is not realized
that a removed line was doubled
up with another. Still, I do not
hesitate to use such methods,and
have, if the situation demands!

                         Brian

the latest rumours from the man

version but it's nearly finished
now.The only big work to be done
is writing the new documentation
- I really want to finish it all

"The new version will include

are emulation of some special

ion and Multiface 128 emulation.
And the new version can load

UNIDOS "KEYWORD" rejection: I discovered this "problem" when I first started using the DOS and thought that my own solution of modifying the OUTLET basic so it would load the CODE suffix files [used in early issues - Ed] WITHOUT having to rename every file may be of interest. If you did rename the files on the disk then there is also the problem that all the file names in the look-up table in the menu rout- ine also have to renamed.

The files with the CODE suffix are in the main text files that are loaded from the BASIC rout- ine that forms the menu screen.

A relative small mod overcomes most of the problems although there may be odd programs that after loading the BASIC go on and load a CODE file and so will need to be altered on similar lines.

Typical loading routines look like...

LOAD d*; C$(PEEK NIF) CODE  or.. LOAD d*;(CODE K$ - CODE "@")CODE

Using Issue No.15 as an example, the BASIC to load the code file is in line 300 and needs to be changed to:

LOAD d*;C$(CODE K$-CODE "@", TO 9) +"*" CODE.

The idea is possible because the "CODE" keyword character part of the name is always at the 10th position. The modified loading routine therefore removes the original CODE character from the file name and substitutes "*" (wild card - you could use "?" instead) so when loading a file the 10th character in the file name on disk is ignored.

Obviously the files still load OK on GDOS. Because each issue uses a fairly standard block of code, all that is needed is to write a new line and save it to disk. It can then be MERGED into each issue to replace the exist- ing line and the modified BASIC resaved (look around line 9980 for the +D erase and resave).

The "advantages" I can live without, the "disadvantages" were a problem. At least "upgrades" that only modify the BOOT file are no real problem as it is easy to BOOT with either system.

I am at moment considering three options to overcome the problems and enable me to have both ROMs installed and simply switch in one required.I have decided hard switching is all I need as it is most unlikely I would need or want to switch ROMs from soft- ware and that each needs a diff- erent BOOT file.

Option 1 is to make up a PCB with sockets to take both ROM chips that plugs into existing ROM socket (takes up lot of room, covers will no longer fit properly but things can be restored to original).

Option 2 is to solder the two ROMs together leaving appropr- iate pins free to select which required (two dud ROMs if things go wrong! Cover will still not go back on, not easily restored to normal).

Option 3 put both ROM codes onto one IC that plugs into existing socket with few mods. approp- riate half selected by simple switching.

Option 3 is my favoured option. I have yet to consult a local friendly firm to see if they can do this and, more importantly, at what cost. The method allows easy restoration to normal and the original ROMS are left intact and safely stored).

QL RGB socket...

YES, this is the same as the Spectrum for RGB, (pins 7,6,8) comp sync (4) and earth pin (2). The output is at 5V TTL level so similar to the 128 and +2. The +3 is at SCART (1V) level.

Malcolm Perry

Dear Brian/Ron,

Due to a severe shortage in the ideas department I thought I'd examine those CODE-IN-REMs that are a regular feature of OUTLET programs.

My findings are that you use the sysvar 'NEXTLIN' and a negative offset to find the code start address. This address is always (?) the first location after the CHR$ 128 that you use to 'hide' the code. I also note that some- times you use leading zeros so as to be able to adjust the offset anywhere between 0 and 9999 without upsetting things.

However, have you considered sysvar CH-ADD at 23645/6 as a reference? eg.. 9993 RANDOMIZE USR VAL"PEEK

```text
23637 +256 * PEEK 23638 - 0099":
```

REM CODE This moves the assembler file (below) to 60000. After a USR command, an entry to the code sys var CH-ADD points to where the colon is that precedes the REM (or RETURN command). If you allow NN bytes in the REM for an identifier name and the flashing code as well as CHR$ 13 + 128 then... LD HL,(23645); find colon LD BC,NN     ;get forward offset ADD HL,BC    ;get 1st code byte JP (HL)      ;go to it. ..will kick your code into life.

You would then have no more neg- ative offsets to calculate!!

All you need is to get those 8 bytes of code into RAM using NXTLIN(!)and then any subsequent code-in-rem in that program can be started by calling the address in RAM where those eight bytes of code are stored. Thus you'd have line 9993 as previous which moves the 8 code start bytes to say 60000 then...

9994 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 1 9995 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 2 9996 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 3

...and thus you have a generic method of finding that first code byete following CHR$ 128.

I hope yu can follow all this.If not,let me know and I'll try and clarify or even put a working demo together.

I note Chris Oliver made mention of my STRIPPER program in OUT- WORK #83 as being in the current issue. I suspect he is thinking ahead (?) as I can't find it.

Can I just mention your AUTOLOAD program? If you examine line 9 you'll note a GO SUB 1001: GO SUB 1002. Why not remove the RETURN in 1001 and let the GO SUB 1001 process lines 1001 and 1002.

In like vein, that GO SUB 1E3 plus GOSUB 1005 could be cleaned up by renumbering line 1000 to 1004,removing the RETURN in 1004 and then a single GO SUB 1004 will handle lines 1004 and 1005. It saves a few bytes which helps on +3 disks.

I think I've said enough.

Malcolm

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

Those are interesting ideas but I don't think they merit the change...

The advantages I think you see in your code-in-rem method are..

1. Code lines use less memory. 2. No need to calculate offset.

However, No.1 is only effective if one has several lines because of the extra setup line and No.2 is ineffective because we don't actually need to calculate the offset! It is done automatically and effortlessly by REMSTORE in Issue 6!

The disadvantages of your method are...

1. More complicated: You still have all the original lines PLUS an extra line PLUS extra code in memory.

2. Extra check needed to see any new code doesn't clash with setup code and subsequent hassle renumbering ALL the lines if set up code has to be moved.

3. Not self-contained. With our present method, all REMs are totally self-contained and need not rely on links with another line/code.

Your method might be preferred if one had dozens of code lines and used a variable for the address of the setup code, eg..

RND USR X:RETURN:CODE

...which not only saves a bit more memory but if the code needed moving slightly one need only alter the value of X.

As it is, our current method is reasonably trouble-free and you know what they say, if it works, leave it alone! Well, something like that anyway! You know what I mean, unless there is a BIG advantage in a change or the present method causes some great hassle then I say let thing lie!

Your idea of merging of GOSUBs in the loader program is OK in theory but the GOSUBs are self- contained so can be removed or added to with ease at present. However, if you take out a RETURN here and there, one may get an error with any future changes if it is not realized that a removed line was doubled up with another. Still, I do not hesitate to use such methods,and have, if the situation demands!

Ведь если переименовывать файлы на диске, возникает ещё и проблема с тем, что все имена файлов в таблице подстановки меню тоже придётся переименовать.

Файлы с суффиксом CODE — это в основном текстовые файлы, которые загружаются из процедуры на BASIC, формирующей экран меню.

Сравнительно небольшая переделка решает большинство проблем, хотя могут встретиться отдельные программы, которые после загрузки BASIC продолжают подгружать CODE-файл, и их придётся исправить аналогичным образом.

Обычные загрузочные процедуры выглядят так:

```text
LOAD d*; C$(PEEK NIF) CODE
```
или:
```text
LOAD d*;(CODE K$ - CODE "@")CODE
```

Если взять в качестве примера выпуск № 15, то бейсик-строка для загрузки кодового файла находится в строке 300, и её нужно изменить на:

```text
  LOAD d*;C$(CODE K$-CODE "@", TO 9) +"*" CODE.
```

Эта идея реализуема потому, что символ ключевого слова «CODE» в имени всегда находится на 10-й позиции. Модифицированная процедура загрузки убирает оригинальный символ CODE из имени файла и подставляет вместо него «*» (подстановочный знак — можно использовать и «?»), поэтому при загрузке 10-й символ имени файла на диске игнорируется.

Разумеется, под GDOS файлы всё равно загружаются нормально. Так как в каждом выпуске используется довольно стандартный блок кода, всё, что требуется — это написать новую строку и сохранить её на диск. Затем её можно объединять через MERGE с каждым выпуском, заменяя существующую строку, и перезаписывать модифицированный BASIC (поищите в районе строки 9980 команды стирания и перезаписи для +D).

Однако задумывались ли вы об использовании системной переменной CH-ADD по адресу 23645/6 в качестве точки отсчёта? Например:

```text
9993 RANDOMIZE USR VAL"PEEK 23637 +256 * PEEK 23638 - 0099": REM CODE
```

Это перемещает файл ассемблера (ниже) в адрес 60000. После команды USR и перехода к коду системная переменная CH-ADD указывает на двоеточие, предшествующее REM (или команду RETURN). Если вы выделите в REM NN байт под имя-идентификатор и мигающий код, а также CHR$ 13 + 128, то:

```text
LD HL,(23645) ; найти двоеточие
LD BC,NN      ; получить смещение вперёд
ADD HL,BC     ; получить 1-й байт кода
JP (HL)       ; перейти к нему.
```
...и ваш код оживёт.

Тогда вам больше не придётся вычислять отрицательные смещения!!

Всё, что вам нужно — это загнать эти 8 байт кода в RAM с помощью NXTLIN (!), а затем любой последующий code-in-rem в этой программе можно запускать простым вызовом адреса в RAM, где хранятся эти восемь байт. Таким образом, у вас будет строка 9993, как и раньше, которая перемещает 8 стартовых байтов, скажем, в 60000, а затем...

```text
9994 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 1
9995 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 2
9996 RAND USR 60000: REM CODE 3
```

...и в итоге получается универсальный метод поиска первого байта кода, следующего за CHR$ 128.
